You’re right to be cautious. We already created a script with a dry-run and per-service controls, but here’s a safer, step-by-step way to pinpoint the culprit before disabling anything.

Quick triage
- Compare TTY vs GUI login:
  - Press Ctrl+Alt+F3 to get a text console, log in there.
  - If TTY login is also slow, it’s likely NSS/PAM/back-end (sssd/nslcd/winbind/DNS).
  - If TTY is fast but GUI is slow, suspect the display manager (gdm/lightdm/sddm) or session start.

Find likely offenders
- What’s slow at boot:
  - systemd-analyze blame | grep -E 'gdm|gdm3|lightdm|sddm|sssd|nslcd|winbind|nscd|display-manager'
  - systemd-analyze critical-chain
- Login-related journal:
  - sudo journalctl -b --no-pager -u gdm -u gdm3 -u lightdm -u sddm -u sssd -u nslcd -u nscd -u winbind
  - sudo journalctl -b -g 'pam_sss|pam_unix|sssd|nss|winbind|nslcd|Timed out|timed out|Failed|denied'
- Test NSS latency (common cause of slow logins):
  - time getent passwd "$USER"
  - time id "$USER"
  - time getent group "$USER"
  If these hang, NSS is slow (often DNS/LDAP/AD via sssd/nslcd/winbind).

Check name resolution/DNS
- resolvectl status (or systemd-resolve --status)
- Look for slow/unreachable DNS servers or search domains causing lookups to hang.

Increase logging (temporarily)
- sssd:
  - Edit /etc/sssd/sssd.conf (backup first), add or raise debug_level = 9 under [sssd], [nss], [pam], and your [domain/...].
  - sudo systemctl restart sssd
  - Check /var/log/sssd/sssd_nss.log, sssd_pam.log, and domain logs.
- winbind (Samba):
  - In /etc/samba/smb.conf set log level = 3 (or 5 to be noisier), then sudo systemctl restart winbind; inspect /var/log/samba/log.winbindd*.
- nslcd:
  - nslcd logs to syslog/journal; enable debug with -d in service or config (varies by distro) and check journalctl -u nslcd.

Gradual, reversible testing (no disabling)
- Stop one suspect at a time and test a new login session. Do this from a TTY so you don’t strand your GUI session.
  - sudo systemctl stop sssd
  - sudo systemctl stop nslcd
  - sudo systemctl stop winbind
  - sudo systemctl stop nscd
  - For display managers, be careful: stopping gdm/lightdm/sddm will end the GUI. Only do this from a TTY:
    - sudo systemctl stop gdm   (or gdm3/lightdm/sddm)
- Revert:
  - sudo systemctl start <service>

- Preview what it would do:
  - sudo /workspace/disable_auth_services.sh --dry-run
- Try one service at a time and don’t mask:
  - sudo /workspace/disable_auth_services.sh --no-mask sssd
  - sudo /workspace/disable_auth_services.sh --restore  (to bring back prior state)

Tell me:
- Your distro and version (Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL, Debian, etc.).
- Whether you rely on LDAP/AD/domain logins (so we don’t cut off access).
- Your display manager (gdm, lightdm, sddm).

+      echo "Aborted." >&2

+    fi
+  fi

+DRY_RUN="no"
+RESTORE="no"
+NO_MASK="no"
+FORCE="no"
+

+

+  case "$1" in

+    fi

+  if [[ "$prev_enabled" == "masked" ]]; then prev_masked=yes; fi

+  if systemctl is-active --quiet "$svc"; then prev_active=yes; fi
+
+  echo -e "$svc\t$prev_enabled\t$prev_masked\t$prev_active" >>"$STATE_FILE"

+  if [[ "$DRY_RUN" == "yes" ]]; then
